title: 3.5.8 Lab: Dot vs. Bracket — When You're Forced to Bracket
description: Read a key with a space and a key held in a variable, and print every key/value pair with Object.keys. Auto-graded.

steps.title: Build an object with a spaced key
steps.instructions: Create an object called laptop that has at least one property whose key contains a space, written in quotes, such as "screen size".

steps.title: Read the spaced key with brackets
steps.instructions: Print the value of the property with the space in its name. Use square brackets with the quoted key.

steps.title: Store a key name in a variable
steps.instructions: Create a variable that holds the name of one of the object's properties, as a string.

steps.title: Read that property with brackets
steps.instructions: Use the variable inside square brackets to print that property's value.

steps.title: Walk every key
steps.instructions: Use Object.keys with a loop to print every key and its value, using brackets to fetch each value. Use Object.keys with a for...of loop; for...in is not part of this course.

requirements.title: square bracket access used
requirements.description: Reads a property with square brackets. Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: Square brackets go after the object name and hold the key, like object["key"] or object[variable].

requirements.title: spaced key reached in brackets
requirements.description: Reads laptop with square brackets and a quoted key that contains a space. Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: A key with a space cannot be written with a dot. Put the quoted key in square brackets.

requirements.title: Object.keys walked with a loop
requirements.description: A loop goes over Object.keys(laptop), fetches each value with the key in square brackets, and prints it. A loop inside a function nobody calls never runs. Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: Use Object.keys: for (const key of Object.keys(laptop)), and inside the loop print laptop[key]. Object.entries and for...in do not count here. A while loop over the keys, or a helper the loop calls, counts too (checked when you press Run).

requirements.title: key name in a variable, read with brackets and printed
requirements.description: A variable holds one key name as a string, and console.log prints the value read with that variable in square brackets (directly, or through a variable that is then printed). Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: Store a key name in a variable as a string (const wanted = "ram";), then print the value with the variable in square brackets: console.log(laptop[wanted]).

requirements.title: laptop has a key with a space in it
requirements.description: After the code runs, laptop is an object and one of its keys contains a space. Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: Give laptop a key with a space in it, written in quotes: "screen size": 13.

checks.fail: laptop should be an object literal: const laptop = { brand: "Framework", "screen size": 13 };
None of laptop's keys has a space in it. Add one, written in quotes, like "screen size": 13.

requirements.title: laptop's values are printed by reads that run
requirements.description: Code that runs prints the spaced key's value read with brackets, the value read with the key held in a variable, and, from a loop, every key of laptop with its value. A printed undefined names the read that found nothing. Help: 3.5.6 (Square Brackets and Computed Keys)
requirements.hint: Print laptop["screen size"], then laptop[wanted] where wanted holds a key name, then loop over Object.keys(laptop) printing each key and laptop[key].

checks.fail: Nothing was printed by code that runs. A console.log inside a function nobody calls, or behind a test that is never true, prints nothing.
A printed line says undefined: a read found nothing. Check the spelling of each name you read.
The spaced key's value is not printed by code that runs. Print it with brackets and the quoted key: console.log(laptop["screen size"]).
No console.log that runs prints a value read with a key held in a variable. Store a key name, const wanted = "ram";, then print laptop[wanted].
No loop prints every key of laptop with its value. Loop over Object.keys(laptop) and, inside the loop, print the key and laptop[key].
